newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania needs austerity to avoid Bulgaria's fate - PM.
newsitem.headline: Romania needs austerity to avoid Bulgaria's fate - PM.

text.p: Romania's Prime Minister Victor Ciorbea called on Friday for support for tough reforms drafted by his new centrist government, which he said were vital if his country wanted to avoid a Bulgaria-type crisis.
"There is no alternative. The only solution is to adopt these tough short- and medium-term steps," Ciorbea told a meeting with leaders of his National Peasant Party.

"Otherwise, we might go down the same path as Bulgaria," he added. "But I am certain that we can avoid that course and that we will have the strength needed to persuade our fellow countrymen of the necessity of those reforms."

In neighbouring Bulgaria, 30 days of mass protests fuelled by economic hardship came to an end after President Petar Stoyanov, elected on the opposition ticket last November, brokered an agreement with the ruling ex-communists to hold early polls on April 19.

Ciorbea gave fellow party leaders a foretaste of sweeping economic moves, coupled with social protection steps, which his coalition government has drafted together with International Monetary Fund and World Bank experts.
Planned policy steps would include price liberalisation, faster privatisation of the economy and streamlining of loss-making communist era industries.
Ciorbea said he would announce the fine print of the reform package, "designed to stabilise the economy and restructure key sectors", during a news conference next Monday.
Bucharest is seeking up to $1.0 billion in total loans from the IMF and World Bank. Both lenders had withheld credits for Romania last year.

Local analysts say the outcome of last November's vote -- when ex-communists were removed from office for the first time in seven years -- reflects many Romanians' weariness with the country's slow and painful transition to the free market.
Romanians, whose purchasing power was halved in the post-communist era, now earn an average of some $60 a month.
Ciorbea's new coalition government faces the difficult task of keeping trade unions at bay, while bringing bulging deficits and inflation under control.

"We cannot achieve these reforms unless we ensure social peace, which is absolutely necessary." said Ciorbea, who won his reputation as a no-nonsense labour leader in hard-fought negotiations with previous post-communist governments.

He announced plans to cut the state budget gap to 4.5 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) this year, from 5.8 percent in 1996, and to slash the 1997 trade gap to $1.4 billion, from $2.5 billion in 1996.

Trade ministry officials subsequently told Reuters that the trade deficit figure of $2.5 billion quoted by Ciorbea was in CIF prices, compared to latest trade data, in FOB prices, which had put that deficit at $1.54 billion.
One-third of the 1997 budget would go to social protection, Ciorbea said: "We could't afford more in the present situation.
The 1997 budget bill -- a plank of loan talks with the IMF and World Bank -- would be submitted to parliament later this month, he said.

The government said later on Friday it had reached agreement "in principle" with the Fund, World Bank and European Union, after more than a month of loan talks. Details of those accords would be disclosed next Monday.
